draft.title: What sustainability means
card: Sustainability means meeting the needs of people today without harming the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.

It covers three areas: the environment, the economy and society. The environment is the natural world. The economy is how goods, services and jobs are produced. Society is the wellbeing of people and communities.
The three areas are linked. A choice that helps one area can harm another, so sustainable decisions try to weigh all three.
The idea looks ahead. A way of living is not sustainable if it uses up resources or damages ecosystems so that later generations are left with less.
draft.remember: Sustainability means meeting today's needs while leaving future generations able to meet theirs.

a.q: Which choice best shows the idea of sustainability?
opts: Fishing at a rate that lets fish stocks recover each year
Fishing as much as possible to maximise profit this year
Banning all fishing so that no one is ever affected
Fishing only in places that are close to the port
a.why: Fishing at a rate that lets stocks recover meets present needs and keeps fish for the future. Maximising profit now may leave nothing for later generations. A ban on all fishing ignores the needs of people today, so it does not weigh them.
a.clue: Look for the choice that serves people now and later.

b.q: A council in regional NSW clears a large area of bushland for a new factory. The factory creates many jobs, but the cleared land cannot recover and local species lose their habitat. Why is this decision not sustainable?
opts: It helps the economy but harms the environment long term
It creates jobs, and jobs are never part of sustainability
It affects society only, because no one lives in bushland
It harms the environment, so the economy cannot be involved
b.why: Sustainability weighs the environment, the economy and society together. The jobs help the economy and people now, but the lasting loss of habitat harms the environment and future generations. Jobs do matter to sustainability, so the claim that they do not is wrong.
b.clue: Check which of the three areas gains and which loses.

a.best: Fishing at a rate that lets fish stocks recover each year

b.best: It helps the economy but harms the environment long term

problems.detail: The right option stands out. Every distractor uses an absolute ('only', 'never', 'cannot') or a plainly false claim ('no one lives in bushland'), so a student can pick the only measured option without understanding the three areas. This is also very easy for Year 12 HSC.

check.summary: The card and both answers are correct. In question b the distractors are so absolute and implausible that the right option is easy to spot without knowing the idea, so they should be made more plausible.

a.q: Which choice best shows the idea of sustainability?
opts: Fishing at a rate that lets fish stocks recover each year
Fishing as much as possible to maximise profit this year
Banning all fishing so that fish stocks are fully protected
Fishing only in places that are close to the port
a.why: Fishing at a rate that lets stocks recover meets present needs and keeps fish for the future. Maximising profit now may leave nothing for later generations. A ban on all fishing ignores the needs of people today, so it does not weigh all three areas.
a.clue: Look for the choice that serves people now and later.

b.q: A council in regional NSW clears a large area of bushland for a new factory. The factory creates many jobs, but the cleared land cannot recover and local species lose their habitat. Which judgement about this decision is correct?
opts: Not sustainable: later generations are left with less
Not sustainable: the environment ranks above jobs
Sustainable: jobs help both the economy and society
Sustainable: the harm falls on wildlife, not on people
b.why: The jobs help the economy and society now, but the lasting damage to the ecosystem leaves later generations with less, so the decision is not sustainable. It is tempting to say the environment outranks jobs, but sustainability weighs all three areas rather than ranking one first.
b.clue: Think about the people who come after the factory is built.
